opus-5.5.text:
I think it really comes down to a culture that has built up over decades. If you look back, Berkeley has a long lineage: BSD Unix, then Postgres, RISC-V on the hardware side, and more recently Spark and Ray. vLLM grew out of that same environment. When you're inside it, you feel that this is just how things are done, not a coincidence.

A few things stand out to me.

First, the lab model. Berkeley has these labs, like AMPLab, then RISELab, now Sky Computing Lab, that run on roughly five-year cycles. Each one gathers faculty from systems, machine learning, databases, and other areas around one big problem. Because the labs are funded partly by industry sponsors, there's a constant flow of real problems from companies into the lab. You aren't writing a paper in a vacuum. You're hearing directly from people who say, "This is what's breaking in our production systems." That pushes students to build things people actually need.

Second, the definition of research output. At many places a paper is the end product. At Berkeley, especially in systems, there's a strong belief that the artifact matters as much as the paper, sometimes more. If people use your system, that's the strongest validation of your idea. Professors like Ion Stoica have shown many times that you can take a research prototype, open-source it, build a community, and it becomes infrastructure. Students see that path and believe it's achievable, and that belief is very important.

Third, open source is treated as the default, not an afterthought. With vLLM, the PagedAttention idea was the research contribution, but what made the project matter was that we released it early, made it easy to use, and then spent enormous effort on the unglamorous work: supporting new models within days, fixing bugs, reviewing community PRs, working with hardware vendors. Many academic projects die after the paper is accepted. Berkeley's tradition is that the paper is the beginning.

And finally, timing and taste. A lot of these projects hit an inflection point. Spark arrived when big data processing was exploding, and vLLM arrived right after ChatGPT, when everyone suddenly needed to serve large models efficiently and nobody had a good open solution. Part of the culture is training your instinct to sense where the field is moving and be ready with something solid when the moment comes.

So I wouldn't call it magic. It's a combination of industry-connected labs, advisors who value real-world impact, and a community that sees maintaining open-source software as legitimate, respectable work for researchers. When all of that comes together, projects that start in a university lab can end up running in data centers all over the world.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. I think the first thing to say is that this tradition is real, and it is remarkably consistent. If you look back, you have BSD, Postgres, Spark, Mesos, Ray, and now vLLM. Each of those started as a research project and ended up as something companies actually run in production. That is not luck. There is a culture behind it.

From my own experience working on vLLM, I would describe the Berkeley approach in a few parts.

First, the problem selection is systems-oriented and grounded in real pain. Berkeley people are very good at asking: what is the bottleneck that everyone is hitting right now, and nobody has solved well? For vLLM, that was LLM serving. Everyone had a model, nobody could serve it efficiently. Memory was wasted, throughput was low. PagedAttention came from looking at that problem the way an operating systems person would, borrowing the idea of virtual memory and paging. The academic contribution and the practical value were the same thing.

Second, there is a strong belief that a paper is not the end product. The code is. At many places, you publish, you release a prototype, and you move on. At Berkeley, especially in the labs that came out of AMPLab and RISELab and now Sky Computing Lab, the expectation is that you keep maintaining it, you answer issues, you accept pull requests, you build a community. That is a lot of unglamorous engineering work that does not directly give you a PhD. But the faculty support it, and the students take pride in it.

Third, Berkeley is physically and socially close to industry. People from the big labs and startups come to meetings, give feedback, and sometimes contribute code. So the project is constantly tested against production needs very early. When vLLM added features like continuous batching, quantization support, or distributed inference, a lot of that was driven by what users told us they needed, not by what would make a nice paper.

Fourth, I think the open-source licensing culture matters. Berkeley historically chose permissive licenses. The BSD license is literally named after Berkeley. That lowers the barrier for companies to adopt the project, and once they adopt it, they have an incentive to contribute back rather than fork and maintain privately.

Finally, there is a kind of generosity in the culture. The project is not treated as one person's asset. Students graduate, new students join, and the project continues. Spark became Databricks, Ray became Anyscale, but the open-source projects stayed open and kept growing. Commercialization and open source are not seen as opposites. The company succeeds because the open-source project is healthy.

So if I summarize, Berkeley's tradition is: pick the real bottleneck, treat code as the deliverable, stay close to industry, license permissively, and keep the community bigger than any individual. When you do that consistently for decades, you end up producing infrastructure.

astra-6.text:
I think Berkeley has a strong tradition of treating systems research as something people should actually be able to use. You don’t just propose an idea and publish a paper; you build a system, release it, and let other people test whether the idea works for their problems.

Open source is important because it allows that work to grow beyond the original research team. Users bring workloads you didn’t anticipate, find limitations, and contribute improvements. Over time, a research prototype can become something much more useful through that collaboration.

But I wouldn’t say becoming industrial infrastructure happens automatically. There’s a lot of work between a good research idea and a dependable system—documentation, compatibility, maintenance. To me, the strength of that tradition is that research ambition and practical usefulness can reinforce each other. Real users expose new research questions, and research gives you new ways to solve their problems.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is that Berkeley treats research as something people should be able to build on. A paper can introduce an idea, but an open-source project lets other people test that idea, improve it, and use it in settings the original researchers never imagined.

Becoming infrastructure takes more than releasing code, though. You have to listen to users, make the system reliable, and create a community where people outside the university can contribute. That also creates a valuable feedback loop: practical problems lead to new research questions, and research helps solve those problems.

So I see it as a combination of ambitious research and a willingness to do the engineering that makes the research useful. The project really succeeds when it can grow beyond the people who started it.
